short: A passive debt fund that holds bonds maturing around one fixed date and pays investors back when that date arrives.
kid: Imagine a jar with a label that says 'open on your birthday'. You put coins in now, and on that day you get them back with a little extra they earned while waiting.
detail: A target maturity fund (TMF) is an open-ended passive debt fund, run as an index fund or ETF, that tracks a bond index whose holdings all mature close to a set date, such as April 2030. It holds the bonds, collects interest and pays everything out at maturity, when the fund closes. Because the portfolio's remaining life shrinks every year (it 'rolls down'), its sensitivity to interest-rate moves falls over time. An investor who holds until maturity earns roughly the portfolio's yield to maturity at the time of buying, less expenses, whatever rates do in between. In India, TMFs grew after the Bharat Bond ETF launch in 2019 and mostly hold government securities, state development loans and AAA-rated PSU bonds. Common confusion: a TMF is not a fixed deposit. Returns are not guaranteed, and selling before maturity means accepting that day's market price, which can be a loss.
example: Say an investor puts ₹5,00,000 into a target maturity fund maturing in 4 years when its portfolio yield is 7.2% and its expense ratio is 0.2%. Held to maturity, the money grows at roughly 7.0% a year to about ₹6,55,398 (₹5,00,000 × 1.07^4), before tax.
formula: Approximate annual return if held to maturity = Yield to maturity at purchase − Expense ratio

short: An equity mutual fund that must put most of its money into the biggest listed companies, in India the top 100 by market value.
kid: Think of a toy box where you only keep toys from the biggest, best-known toy makers. They are not always the most exciting, but they rarely break.
detail: A large-cap fund is an equity mutual fund that invests mainly in the largest listed companies. Under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025, large caps are the 1st to 100th companies by full market capitalisation, using a list AMFI updates every six months, and a large-cap fund must keep at least 80% of its assets in them. These firms are usually established market leaders, so large-cap funds tend to fall less than mid- or small-cap funds in downturns but also rise less in strong rallies. Because the top 100 stocks are heavily researched, many active large-cap funds struggle to beat their benchmark after fees, which is why low-cost index funds on the Nifty 50 or Nifty 100 are popular alternatives. Common confusion: 'bluechip' in a fund's name is marketing language; the SEBI category, not the name, sets the rules.
example: Say ABC Large Cap Fund manages ₹10,000 crore. It must keep at least ₹8,000 crore (80%) in the top 100 companies, leaving at most ₹2,000 crore for mid caps, small caps, debt or cash.

short: An equity mutual fund that invests mostly in medium-sized listed companies, in India those ranked 101 to 250 by market value.
kid: Think of a garden of plants that are no longer tiny seedlings but not yet tall trees. They can still grow a lot, but a strong wind shakes them more than the big trees.
detail: A mid-cap fund is an equity mutual fund focused on medium-sized companies. Under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025, mid caps are the 101st to 250th companies by full market capitalisation, based on AMFI's half-yearly list, and a mid-cap fund must invest at least 65% of its assets in them. The rest can go into large caps, small caps, debt or cash. Mid-sized firms often have room to grow faster than market leaders while being more established than small caps, so mid-cap funds have historically offered higher long-run return potential with sharper falls in bad years. Their stocks can be less liquid, so heavy inflows or outflows matter more. Common confusion: 'mid-cap' is a rank, not a fixed rupee size; as markets rise, the value of the 250th company rises too, and stocks move between categories at each AMFI review.
example: Say XYZ Midcap Fund has ₹2,000 crore of assets. It must hold at least ₹1,300 crore (65%) in companies ranked 101 to 250 by market value, and can place the other ₹700 crore elsewhere.

short: An equity mutual fund that invests mostly in smaller listed companies, in India those ranked 251st and below by market value.
kid: Imagine planting lots of tiny seeds. Some will grow into huge sunflowers, some will stay small and a few will not grow at all, so you need patience.
detail: A small-cap fund is an equity mutual fund that invests at least 65% of its assets in small companies, defined under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025 as those ranked 251st and below by full market capitalisation. Small companies can grow much faster than large ones, but they are also more fragile, with weaker finances and thinner trading. That makes small-cap funds the most volatile diversified equity category, with deep falls in bear markets, so they suit investors with long horizons. Liquidity is the key risk for the fund itself: if many investors redeem at once, the manager may have to sell shares that trade in small volumes. Since 2024, Indian fund houses publish regular stress tests showing how long it would take to sell part of the portfolio, and some have limited lump-sum inflows when valuations looked stretched. Common confusion: a small-cap fund can itself be very large.
example: Say PQR Small Cap Fund manages ₹4,000 crore. At least ₹2,600 crore (65%) must sit in companies ranked 251st or lower, and if small caps fall 30% in a sell-off, that portion alone drops by ₹780 crore.

short: An equity mutual fund that can invest in companies of any size, large, mid or small, in whatever mix the manager chooses.
kid: It is like a lunchbox you can fill with a big sandwich or lots of small snacks, in any mix you like, as long as most of it is proper food.
detail: A flexi-cap fund is an equity mutual fund that must keep at least 65% of its assets in equities but has no limits on how much goes into large, mid or small companies, under SEBI's rules as of 2025. SEBI created the category in November 2020, soon after it redefined multi-cap funds to require minimum holdings in each size bucket; many old multi-cap funds then switched to flexi-cap to keep their freedom. The manager can tilt towards large caps when smaller stocks look expensive and add mid and small caps when they look cheap. That flexibility makes flexi-cap funds a popular single core holding, but results depend heavily on the manager's calls. Common confusion: flexi-cap and multi-cap sound alike, yet only multi-cap funds must hold at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps; a flexi-cap fund could legally hold 90% large caps.
example: Say a ₹1,000 crore flexi-cap fund holds ₹700 crore in large caps, ₹150 crore in mid caps, ₹100 crore in small caps and ₹50 crore in cash. Its equity share is 95% (₹950 crore), well above the 65% minimum, and no size bucket has a floor.

short: An equity mutual fund that must spread its money across large, mid and small companies, with a minimum share in each size group.
kid: Imagine a fruit bowl that must always have some apples, some bananas and some grapes. You can add extra of any fruit, but none can ever be missing.
detail: A multi-cap fund is an equity mutual fund that must invest across all three size groups. Under SEBI's rules as of 2025, it keeps at least 75% of assets in equities, with at least 25% each in large-cap (top 100), mid-cap (101 to 250) and small-cap (251 and below) companies. The remaining 25% can go wherever the manager chooses. SEBI set these floors in September 2020 because many funds labelled multi-cap were holding mostly large caps. The fixed minimums give built-in exposure to smaller companies, which raises both return potential and volatility compared with a flexi-cap or large-cap fund. Because the small-cap floor must always be met, a big multi-cap fund can find it harder to put money to work in less liquid stocks. Common confusion: before 2020, multi-cap meant roughly what flexi-cap means today, so older articles and return comparisons may describe a different kind of portfolio.
example: Say a ₹1,000 crore multi-cap fund. It must hold at least ₹250 crore each in large, mid and small caps (₹750 crore in total), and the remaining ₹250 crore can go into any size bucket, debt or cash.

short: A mutual fund that puts most of its money into companies from a single industry, such as banking, pharma or technology.
kid: Imagine collecting only toy cars. If everyone suddenly loves cars, your collection shines, but if cars go out of fashion, the whole collection loses its sparkle together.
detail: A sector fund is an equity mutual fund that invests mainly in one industry, such as banking, pharma, IT or FMCG. Under SEBI's categorisation rules as of 2025, sectoral and thematic funds share one category and must keep at least 80% of assets in the chosen sector or theme, and a fund house may run several of them. Because every holding faces the same business cycle, regulation and demand drivers, returns swing far more than in diversified funds: a sector can lead the market for years and then lag for years. Investors use sector funds for tactical bets rather than as core holdings, and the timing of entry and exit matters a lot. Common confusion: a sector fund is narrower than a thematic fund, which can span several related sectors, and a 'banking and PSU fund' is actually a debt fund, not a banking-sector equity fund.
example: Say a ₹500 crore pharma fund must keep at least ₹400 crore (80%) in pharma and healthcare stocks. If those stocks fall 20% in a year when the broad market is flat, that ₹400 crore portion loses ₹80 crore.

short: A mutual fund that invests in companies linked by one broad idea, such as consumption, manufacturing or ESG, across several industries.
kid: Imagine a birthday party where everything is about space: rocket cake, star balloons, astronaut games. Lots of different things, all chosen because they fit the same idea.
detail: A thematic fund is an equity mutual fund built around a broad idea rather than a single industry, for example consumption, infrastructure, manufacturing, digital India, PSU companies or ESG. A theme can pull in several sectors: an infrastructure fund might own cement, power, construction and capital-goods companies. In India, SEBI groups thematic and sectoral funds in one category, and under the rules as of 2025 they must keep at least 80% of assets in stocks that match the stated theme. Fund houses love launching them when a story is popular, so many arrive near peak excitement. They are more diversified than sector funds but still concentrated, so results depend on whether the theme plays out and whether it was already priced in. Common confusion: a catchy theme is not an edge in itself; check the actual holdings and how much they overlap with funds you already own.
example: Say a ₹800 crore infrastructure fund must hold at least ₹640 crore (80%) in theme stocks, spread as ₹200 crore in power, ₹180 crore in construction, ₹160 crore in capital goods and ₹100 crore in cement.

short: A mutual fund that invests in shares or other funds listed abroad, letting investors own US or global companies from home.
kid: It is like getting toys from a pen-friend in another country. You can enjoy toys your town does not have, but how much they seem worth can change on the way back and forth.
detail: An international fund invests in securities listed outside the investor's home country. Indian versions either buy foreign shares directly or act as feeder funds, a kind of fund of funds that puts nearly all its money into one overseas parent fund or ETF, for example one tracking the Nasdaq-100 or S&P 500. They add exposure to companies and economies missing from Indian markets. Returns have two parts: the foreign market's move and the change in the rupee against that currency, so a falling rupee boosts rupee returns. Indian mutual funds face an industry-wide overseas investment cap set by SEBI ($7 billion, plus $1 billion for overseas ETFs, under the rules as of 2025). When that cap was hit in early 2022, SEBI told fund houses to stop fresh subscriptions. Common confusion: tax treatment differs from domestic equity funds, so check the current rules before comparing post-tax returns.
example: Say a US index fund gains 10% in dollar terms in a year while the rupee weakens from ₹80 to ₹84 per dollar, a 5% move. An Indian investor's return is 1.10 × 1.05 − 1 = 15.5%, so ₹1,00,000 becomes ₹1,15,500.
formula: Rupee return = (1 + Return in foreign currency) × (1 + Change in exchange rate) − 1

short: A fund that does not buy shares or bonds directly but invests in other funds, such as mutual funds or ETFs.
kid: Imagine a big basket that holds several smaller baskets of fruit. You carry one basket, but inside you get a bit of every fruit from all the small ones.
detail: A fund of funds (FoF) invests in units of other funds instead of directly in shares or bonds. In India, common types are multi-asset FoFs that mix equity, debt and gold funds, FoFs that wrap an ETF so investors without a demat account can invest, and international feeder funds that invest in an overseas fund. The appeal is ready-made diversification and rebalancing in one product. The catch is two layers of costs: the FoF's own expense ratio plus the expenses of the underlying funds, although SEBI caps the combined total. Globally, funds of hedge funds and private equity funds of funds pool money across many managers for investors who cannot access them individually. Common confusion: an FoF is not automatically more diversified than a single fund; if its underlying funds hold the same stocks, you own the same companies several times over while paying more.
example: Say an FoF charges 0.5% a year and the funds it holds charge 1.0% on average. An investor with ₹2,00,000 pays about 1.5% in total, or ₹3,000 a year, compared with ₹2,000 for owning the underlying funds directly.
formula: Total cost ≈ FoF expense ratio + Weighted average expense ratio of the underlying funds

short: A fund that automatically shifts from riskier shares to safer bonds as a chosen year, usually the investor's retirement, gets closer.
kid: When you are far from home you can run and jump along the way, but as you get close to the door you slow down and walk carefully so you do not trip.
detail: A target-date fund holds a mix of equity and debt that changes automatically along a preset schedule called the glide path. A fund labelled 2055 starts with mostly shares, since its investors have decades to ride out falls, and steadily moves towards bonds and cash as 2055 approaches, to protect savings when they are about to be needed. The investor simply picks the year closest to their retirement and the fund handles rebalancing. In the US these funds are the default option in many 401(k) retirement plans. In India, the closest equivalent is the 'auto choice' lifecycle option in the National Pension System, where the equity share falls with age, and a few mutual funds offer similar retirement products. Common confusion: two funds with the same target year can follow very different glide paths, and reaching the target date neither guarantees the money nor means the fund stops holding equities.
example: Say a 2055 fund holds 90% equities and 10% bonds today and its glide path ends at 40% equities in 2055. On a ₹10 lakh balance, the equity part would fall from ₹9 lakh now to ₹4 lakh by then if the balance stayed unchanged.

short: A private, lightly regulated investment fund for wealthy and institutional investors that can borrow, short sell and use derivatives to seek profits.
kid: Imagine a club of clever grown-ups who play many kinds of guessing games to win prizes, even guessing that some things will go down instead of up. Only grown-ups with lots of coins can join.
detail: A hedge fund is a privately offered pooled fund that can use strategies most mutual funds cannot: short selling, heavy leverage, derivatives, concentrated bets and hard-to-sell assets. The name comes from early funds that 'hedged' market risk by pairing long and short positions, but today many take large directional bets. Because they are sold only to wealthy individuals and institutions, they face lighter disclosure rules, often limit when investors can withdraw, and traditionally charge '2 and 20': a 2% yearly management fee plus 20% of profits, though fees have fallen. Major styles include long-short equity, global macro, event-driven, relative value and multi-strategy. In India, hedge-fund-style vehicles are mostly registered with SEBI as Category III alternative investment funds, with a high minimum ticket under the rules as of 2025. Common confusion: 'hedge' does not mean safe; some hedge funds are far riskier than the stock market.
example: Say a $100 million hedge fund gains $15 million in a year. Under '2 and 20' it takes a $2 million management fee (2% of assets), then 20% of the remaining $13 million gain, or $2.6 million, so investors keep $10.4 million.

short: An investing style that buys shares expected to rise and short sells shares expected to fall, aiming to profit from the gap between them.
kid: Imagine two snails in a race. You say one will be faster than the other. Even if both crawl very slowly, you win as long as your pick finishes first.
detail: Long-short equity is a strategy, used mainly by hedge funds, that holds long positions in stocks the manager expects to do well and short positions in stocks expected to do badly. Short selling means selling borrowed shares and buying them back later cheaper. Two numbers describe such a fund: gross exposure (longs plus shorts), which shows how much capital is at work, and net exposure (longs minus shorts), which shows how much it depends on the overall market's direction. Most run net long, often 30% to 70%. A 130/30 fund is a related product that is 130% long and 30% short, keeping net exposure at 100%. The aim is to profit from stock picking while cushioning market falls. In India, as of 2025, specialised investment funds and some Category III AIFs offer long-short strategies. Common confusion: a long-short fund is not market-neutral unless its net exposure is close to zero.
example: Say a fund has $100 million of capital, $120 million of long positions and $70 million of short positions. Its gross exposure is $190 million (190%) and its net exposure is $50 million (50%), so a 10% market fall would cost roughly $5 million before any stock-picking gains.
formula: Net exposure = Long positions − Short positions; Gross exposure = Long positions + Short positions

short: A hedge fund strategy that bets on big economic trends, such as interest rates, currencies and commodity prices, across countries.
kid: Imagine watching the weather all around the world and guessing where it will rain next. If you guess right, you can bring umbrellas there before anyone else.
detail: Global macro is a hedge fund strategy that takes positions based on views about economies and policy around the world rather than about individual companies. Managers study growth, inflation, central-bank decisions, government finances and politics, then trade the instruments most likely to move: government bonds, interest-rate futures, currencies, stock indices and commodities, usually through liquid derivatives and often with leverage. A fund might buy a country's bonds on expected rate cuts while also betting against its currency. The best-known example is George Soros's Quantum Fund, which bet against the British pound in 1992 and reportedly made about $1 billion when the UK left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. Macro funds tend to do well when big shifts happen, such as rate shocks or currency crises, which makes them useful diversifiers. Common confusion: 'macro' describes the kind of bets, not the fund's size.
example: Say a macro fund expects RBI rate cuts and buys ₹100 crore of 10-year government bonds with a modified duration of 7. If yields fall by 0.5 percentage point, the position gains about ₹3.5 crore (₹100 crore × 7 × 0.5%).

short: An investing approach that seeks profit from company events such as mergers, takeovers, spin-offs, buybacks and bankruptcies.
kid: When a big shop promises to buy a small shop's toys for a set amount, you buy those toys a little cheaper today and wait for the big shop to pay the full amount.
detail: An event-driven strategy tries to profit from price moves caused by specific corporate events rather than from the market's general direction. The best-known form is merger arbitrage, also called risk arbitrage: after an acquirer offers to buy a company, the target's shares usually trade a little below the offer price because the deal might fail or take time. The investor buys the target, sometimes shorting the acquirer in all-stock deals, and earns the gap if the deal closes. Other event-driven plays include spin-offs, demergers, buybacks, open offers, index inclusions, restructurings and distressed debt, often grouped as special situations. Returns depend on judging the odds and timing of the event, not just valuation. Common confusion: merger arbitrage is not risk-free arbitrage; when a deal collapses, for example over regulatory refusal or financing trouble, the target's price can fall far more than the small spread the investor hoped to earn.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at ₹450 after XYZ Ltd offers ₹500 a share in cash. Buying at ₹450 earns ₹50, or 11.1%, if the deal closes; if it collapses and ABC falls back to ₹380, the loss is ₹70 a share.
formula: Merger arbitrage spread = (Offer price − Current target price) / Current target price

short: Passive funds that track rule-based indices which pick or weight stocks by traits like value or low volatility instead of company size.
kid: Instead of picking the biggest children for the team, the coach uses one simple rule, like choosing the fastest runners, and sticks to it every time.
detail: Smart beta refers to index funds and ETFs that follow rule-based indices built on something other than market capitalisation. A normal index weights each company by its market value, so the biggest firms dominate. A smart beta index instead selects or weights stocks by a factor or rule: equal weight, low volatility, momentum, value, quality or dividend yield. The goal is to capture a return pattern that research suggests is rewarded over time, at a cost closer to passive funds than active ones. Indian examples include funds tracking indices such as the Nifty 200 Momentum 30 or Nifty 100 Low Volatility 30. Smart beta sits between active and passive investing: the rules are fixed and transparent, but choosing the rule is an active decision. Common confusion: 'smart' does not mean guaranteed outperformance; factors can lag the market for years, and some need frequent rebalancing, so costs and tracking matter.
example: In an equal-weight version of a 50-stock index, every stock gets 2% (100% / 50), even if in the market-cap version the largest stock is 12% and the smallest 0.5%. Rebalancing back to 2% each quarter makes the fund trim recent winners and add to laggards.

short: Choosing investments by measurable traits, such as cheapness, momentum or quality, that research links to higher returns over long periods.
kid: When picking apples, you might always choose the shiniest ones, or the cheapest, or the ones that ripened fastest. Picking by one simple clue, again and again, is the whole idea.
detail: Factor investing builds portfolios around characteristics, called factors, that help explain why some stocks earn more than others over long periods. The academic roots are the Fama-French models of the 1990s, which added company size and value (stocks that look cheap on measures like price to book) to overall market exposure; later research added momentum, quality (profitable, low-debt firms) and low volatility. A factor investor deliberately tilts towards these traits, either through active stock selection or through rule-based smart beta funds. Factors are also used to analyse any fund: a manager's apparent skill may simply be a tilt towards small or value stocks. Factor returns come in cycles; value, for example, lagged growth stocks for much of the 2010s. Common confusion: a factor premium is a long-run average, not a promise, and crowding into a popular factor can shrink it.
example: Say that over a decade a basket of the cheapest 20% of stocks by price to book returns 14% a year while the most expensive 20% returns 10% a year. The value premium in that sample is 4 percentage points a year.
formula: Fama-French three-factor model: Fund return − Risk-free rate = Alpha + b × (Market return − Risk-free rate) + s × SMB + h × HML

short: The professional who decides what a fund buys, holds and sells, within the fund's stated objective and rules.
kid: Think of a team captain who decides who plays in each match. The team belongs to everyone, but the captain makes the choices.
detail: A fund manager, or portfolio manager, is the person or team responsible for investment decisions in a mutual fund, ETF, pension fund, hedge fund or other pool of money. They decide what to buy and sell and how much to hold, within the fund's mandate, regulations and risk controls, and are usually employed by an asset management company (AMC). In active funds, the manager's skill is what investors pay for; in index funds, the job is mainly to track the index closely and cheaply. In India, SEBI rules as of 2025 require part of the pay of key AMC staff, including fund managers, to be given in units of the schemes they oversee, so their interests line up with investors'. Common confusion: the fund manager is not the distributor or adviser who sells you the fund, and a change of manager can change how a fund behaves.
example: Say a fund manager running a ₹5,000 crore fund decides to cut IT stocks from 15% to 10% of the portfolio. That means selling about ₹250 crore of IT shares (5% of ₹5,000 crore) and reinvesting the money elsewhere.

short: A SEBI-required dial on every Indian mutual fund scheme showing its risk level on a six-step scale from Low to Very High.
kid: It is like the chilli label on a menu: one chilli for mild, lots of chillies for very hot. It tells you how bumpy the ride might be before you choose.
detail: The riskometer is a standard risk label that SEBI requires on every mutual fund scheme in India. Since January 2021, under rules in force as of 2025, it has six levels: Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High. Fund houses work out the level from the actual portfolio using SEBI's scoring method, which looks at things such as company size, volatility and liquidity for equity, and credit quality, interest-rate sensitivity and liquidity for debt. The riskometer is reviewed every month, published on fund house and AMFI websites, and any change must be communicated to unitholders. Debt funds also carry a separate potential risk class matrix showing their maximum credit and interest-rate risk. Most equity funds sit at Very High. Common confusion: the riskometer describes the portfolio's risk, not whether a fund suits you; it says nothing about returns, costs or your goals.
example: An overnight fund lending money for one day is usually labelled Low, level 1 of 6, while a small-cap fund is labelled Very High, level 6 of 6. If a hybrid fund raises its equity share from 40% to 70%, its riskometer may move up a level at the next monthly review.
related: Securities and Exchange Board of India

short: A measure of how much of a fund's holdings are bought and sold in a year, compared with the fund's size.
kid: If you swap a few of your stickers every week, your album keeps changing. Counting how many you swap shows whether you like keeping stickers or changing them often.
detail: The portfolio turnover ratio shows how actively a fund trades. It is usually calculated as the lower of total purchases or total sales over a year, divided by the fund's average net assets. Using the lower figure strips out buying driven by new money coming in and selling driven by redemptions. A ratio of 20% suggests the manager holds stocks for about five years on average; 200% means the portfolio is turned over roughly twice a year. Higher turnover raises hidden costs such as brokerage, taxes and market impact, which the expense ratio does not fully capture, and can signal a short-term or momentum style. Indian fund houses disclose turnover in their monthly factsheets, often separately for the equity portion and the whole portfolio. Common confusion: 100% turnover does not mean every stock was replaced; the manager may have traded a few positions repeatedly while keeping the core untouched.
example: Say ABC Equity Fund bought ₹300 crore and sold ₹250 crore of securities in a year, with average net assets of ₹1,000 crore. Its portfolio turnover ratio is ₹250 crore / ₹1,000 crore = 25%.
formula: Portfolio turnover ratio = Lower of total purchases or total sales in the period / Average net assets in the period

short: Moving a fund's troubled or hard-to-sell assets into a separate portfolio so they do not distort the main fund's value or withdrawals.
kid: If one apple in your basket goes bad, you put it in a separate little bag so it does not spoil the others. If it somehow gets better later, you still get it back.
detail: Side pocketing means moving a distressed or illiquid holding out of a fund's main portfolio into a separate one. In India, SEBI has allowed mutual funds to create a segregated portfolio since December 2018, mainly for debt and money market holdings hit by a credit event, such as a downgrade below investment grade or a default. Every unitholder on the record date gets units in the segregated portfolio equal to their units in the main fund. The main portfolio carries on normally, with fresh purchases and redemptions at a clean NAV, while any money later recovered from the troubled bond is paid only to those who held units on the segregation date. This stops early redeemers from exiting at an inflated NAV and leaving losses to those who stay. Hedge funds use side pockets for illiquid assets too. Common confusion: segregation does not erase the loss; it ring-fences it.
example: Say a debt fund has ₹1,000 crore of assets and 50 crore units, so its NAV is ₹20. A ₹50 crore bond defaults and is side-pocketed, so the main NAV becomes ₹950 crore / 50 crore = ₹19, and an investor with 10,000 units also gets 10,000 segregated units that pay out only if the borrower repays.

short: The money moving into and out of funds over a period, called net inflows when buying exceeds withdrawals and net outflows otherwise.
kid: Think of a bathtub with the tap running and the plug pulled out. If more water pours in than drains away, the tub fills up; if more drains away, the water gets lower.
detail: Fund flows track how much new money investors put into funds and how much they take out through redemptions over a period. Net flow equals gross purchases, including SIPs and lump sums, minus redemptions. Flows are different from changes in assets under management, which also rise or fall with market prices. In India, AMFI publishes monthly flow data by category, and markets watch it closely because steady SIP-driven domestic inflows have become a major source of demand for Indian shares, often offsetting selling by foreign portfolio investors. Globally, flows into or out of ETFs, bond funds and emerging-market funds signal investor mood and can move prices, especially in less liquid assets. Flows tend to chase recent performance, so heavy inflows often arrive after strong rallies. Common confusion: a fund category's assets can grow in a month with net outflows if markets rise enough.
example: Say in a month equity funds receive ₹45,000 crore of purchases and pay out ₹30,000 crore of redemptions, a net inflow of ₹15,000 crore. If the category's assets rose by ₹60,000 crore, the other ₹45,000 crore came from rising market prices.

short: When a supposedly active fund holds nearly the same stocks as its benchmark index while charging higher active-management fees.
kid: Imagine paying extra for a cake the baker says is specially made just for you, when it is really the same cake every shop sells for less.
detail: Closet indexing describes an actively managed fund whose portfolio stays very close to its benchmark index. The fund charges active fees, but because it barely differs from the index, its returns before fees track the index and, after higher costs, it almost certainly lags. Managers may hug the index to avoid the career risk of trailing it badly. It is detected with active share, the percentage of a portfolio that differs from the benchmark, and tracking error, the volatility of return differences; an active share below about 60% is a common warning sign. Regulators in Europe have investigated closet trackers, and in India the rise of low-cost index funds has sharpened the comparison, especially for large-cap funds whose choice of stocks is narrow. Common confusion: low active share is not wrong in itself; it becomes a problem when investors pay active fees for near-index exposure.
example: Say a large-cap fund charges 1.8% a year while an index fund on the same benchmark charges 0.2%. If the active fund's holdings mirror the index, an investor with ₹10 lakh pays about ₹16,000 a year extra (1.6% × ₹10 lakh) for almost the same portfolio.
formula: Active share = 1/2 × Sum of |Weight in fund − Weight in benchmark| across all stocks

short: A SEBI-regulated product, run by mutual fund houses, that can use long-short and other advanced strategies and needs a high minimum investment.
kid: It is like a special room in the toy shop where older children can play trickier games, but only if they bring a big bag of coins to get in.
detail: A specialised investment fund (SIF) is a product category SEBI introduced in 2025 to sit between mutual funds and portfolio management services or alternative investment funds. Eligible mutual fund houses offer them under a separate brand. Under the rules as of 2025, the minimum investment is ₹10 lakh per investor across all SIF strategies of a fund house, and a strategy can take unhedged short positions through derivatives of up to 25% of its net assets, something ordinary mutual fund schemes cannot do. Permitted strategies include equity long-short, sector rotation long-short, debt long-short and hybrid long-short, and some can offer less frequent redemption windows than daily. The aim is to bring more flexible strategies under mutual-fund-style supervision and disclosure. Common confusion: an SIF is not a mutual fund scheme with a new label; it carries more risk, and the ₹10 lakh threshold keeps it away from small retail investors.
example: Say an investor puts ₹10 lakh, the minimum under the rules as of 2025, into an equity long-short SIF strategy with ₹500 crore of assets. The strategy can hold up to ₹125 crore (25%) of unhedged short positions through derivatives, betting on stocks or indices it expects to fall.

short: A government-owned investment fund that invests a country's surplus money, often from oil revenue or reserves, for the long term.
kid: Imagine a town that keeps a special savings jar for everyone. Extra coins go in when times are good, and the jar helps the town's children in the future.
detail: A sovereign wealth fund (SWF) is a state-owned pool of money invested in shares, bonds, real estate, infrastructure and private companies, often worldwide. Many are funded by commodity revenue, like Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, built from oil income and one of the largest investors on earth; others draw on budget surpluses or foreign exchange reserves, as with Singapore's GIC. Other major SWFs include the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. Their goals vary: saving for future generations, steadying the budget when commodity prices fall, or developing the home economy. SWFs are big long-term investors in India, backing roads, infrastructure trusts and listed companies, and India's National Investment and Infrastructure Fund is often described as a quasi-sovereign fund. Common confusion: an SWF is not the central bank's foreign exchange reserve, which must stay safe and liquid; an SWF can take more risk for higher long-run returns.
example: Say a country earns $50 billion a year from oil exports and puts 20% into its sovereign wealth fund, or $10 billion a year. Invested for 20 years at 5% a year, each year's $10 billion grows to about $26.5 billion (1.05^20 ≈ 2.65).

short: A pool of money collected from workers and employers during their working years and invested to pay them income after retirement.
kid: When you are young, you put a few sweets in a jar every week. When you are old, the jar is full, and you can enjoy them even when you no longer go out to get more.
detail: A pension fund collects contributions from employees, employers or both, invests them, and pays benefits after retirement. There are two main designs. In a defined benefit (DB) plan, the employer promises a set pension, often based on salary and years of service, and bears the investment risk; if assets fall short of promised payouts, the plan is underfunded. In a defined contribution (DC) plan, contributions are fixed and the final pot depends on investment returns, so the worker bears the risk. Pension funds such as Canada's CPP Investments and Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund are among the world's biggest investors in shares, bonds and infrastructure. In India, the main systems are the EPFO for salaried workers and the National Pension System regulated by PFRDA, a DC scheme. Common confusion: a 'pension plan' sold by an insurer is a retail product, not the same thing as an institutional pension fund.
example: Say a defined benefit plan pays 2% of final monthly salary for each year of service. A worker retiring after 30 years on ₹1,00,000 a month receives 2% × 30 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹60,000 a month. If the fund holds ₹800 crore against liabilities valued at ₹1,000 crore, its funded ratio is 80%.
formula: Funded ratio = Pension fund assets / Present value of pension liabilities

short: A private firm set up to manage the investments, taxes and affairs of one very wealthy family, or a small group of families.
kid: Imagine a very big family with a huge toy collection. They have a helper whose whole job is to look after the toys, keep them safe and choose new ones.
detail: A family office is a private organisation that manages the wealth of a very rich family. A single family office serves one family; a multi-family office shares the cost of staff and systems across several. Beyond investing, family offices often handle taxes, estate and succession planning, philanthropy, legal matters and even household administration. Because the money is long-term and answers only to the family, family offices can take patient, hard-to-sell positions: direct stakes in private companies, startup funding, real estate and co-investments alongside private equity funds. In India, the number of family offices has grown sharply as promoters, founders and business families formalise their wealth, and they have become active investors in startups, pre-IPO rounds and alternative investment funds. Common confusion: a family office is not a bank's wealth desk; it works only for the family rather than selling products to many clients, though multi-family offices blur that line.
example: Say a family with ₹2,000 crore of wealth sets up a single family office that invests 40% in listed shares (₹800 crore), 25% in private companies (₹500 crore), 20% in bonds (₹400 crore) and 15% in real estate (₹300 crore).

short: A fund's returns measured over many overlapping periods of the same length, showing how consistent it has been rather than just its latest figure.
kid: Instead of judging a friend's running by one race, you watch them run every day for a month. Then you know how fast they usually are, not just on their luckiest day.
detail: Rolling returns measure a fund's annualised return over every possible window of a fixed length within a longer history, such as every 3-year period starting on each day of the last 10 years, and then summarise the results: average, best, worst and how often returns beat a threshold or the benchmark. This contrasts with point-to-point or trailing returns, which use a single start and end date and can look great or awful depending on whether the window happens to begin at a market low or high. Rolling returns reveal consistency, a fund's typical experience and the range of outcomes an investor might actually have had, so they are useful for comparing funds and setting realistic expectations. Common confusion: a high average rolling return can still hide a few very poor windows, so always check the worst figure and how often the fund lagged its benchmark.
example: Say a fund's 1-year returns starting in January, February and March were 10%, 6% and 14%. Its 1-year rolling return averages 10% ((10 + 6 + 14) / 3) with a range of 6% to 14%, while a single point-to-point figure would show only one of these.
formula: Rolling return for each start date t = (NAV at t + n years / NAV at t)^(1/n) − 1, computed for every start date in the history

short: A person or firm registered with AMFI who sells mutual fund schemes to investors and earns commission from the fund houses.
kid: Think of a shopkeeper who sells juice from different juice makers. The makers pay the shopkeeper a little for every bottle sold, so the price includes that small share.
detail: A mutual fund distributor (MFD) helps investors choose, buy and service mutual fund investments. In India, a distributor must pass the NISM Series V-A certification and register with AMFI, which issues an AMFI Registration Number (ARN). Investors who invest through a distributor buy the regular plan of a scheme, whose expense ratio includes the commission the fund house pays the distributor; investors who go direct buy the cheaper direct plan of the same portfolio. Since 2018, SEBI has required an all-trail commission model, banning upfront commissions so that pay is linked to money that stays invested. Banks, national distributors and online platforms all act as distributors. Common confusion: a distributor is not a SEBI-registered investment adviser (RIA); an RIA charges the client a fee for advice and cannot take commissions, while a distributor is paid by the product maker. Both models are legal, but investors should know who pays whom.
example: Say an investor puts ₹5,00,000 into the regular plan of a fund with a 1.6% expense ratio, while the direct plan charges 0.9%. The 0.7% gap costs ₹3,500 a year, much of which reaches the distributor as trail commission.

short: An ongoing yearly commission a fund house pays a distributor, calculated as a percentage of the client's money that stays invested.
kid: Imagine a friend helped you find a good apple tree. For as long as the tree keeps giving apples, a few of them go to that friend every year as a thank-you.
detail: A trail commission is a recurring payment that an asset management company makes to a mutual fund distributor for as long as the investor's money remains in the scheme. It is a percentage of the client's assets, often somewhere around 0.5% to 1% a year for equity funds, and is paid out of the scheme's expense ratio. That is why regular plans, sold through distributors, have higher expense ratios and slightly lower returns than direct plans of the same fund. SEBI moved Indian mutual funds to a full trail model in 2018, banning upfront commissions, so distributors are rewarded for keeping clients invested rather than churning them into new schemes. Consolidated account statements show investors how much commission was paid on their holdings. Common confusion: investors never write a separate cheque for trail; it is deducted daily inside the NAV, so its cost compounds quietly over the years.
example: Say a client has ₹10 lakh in a regular plan that pays a 0.8% yearly trail. The distributor earns about ₹8,000 a year from that client, and a distributor with ₹50 crore of client assets at an average 0.7% earns about ₹35 lakh a year.
formula: Annual trail commission = Client assets in the scheme × Trail rate

short: Selling mutual fund units back to the fund house, which pays the investor their current value minus any exit charge.
kid: It is like taking your toys back out of a shared toy box. You get back your share of whatever is in the box that day.
detail: Redemption is how an investor exits an open-ended mutual fund: the units are sold back to the fund itself, not to another investor, and cancelled. The price is the NAV that applies to the day the request is received before the cut-off time, minus any exit load, and the money reaches the bank account within a few working days under SEBI's timelines. When many investors redeem at once, the fund must sell holdings to raise cash, which can force sales at poor prices and hurt those who stay; this is called redemption pressure. In April 2020, Franklin Templeton wound up six Indian debt schemes after illiquid holdings could not be sold fast enough to meet redemptions. Common confusion: for bonds, redemption means the issuer repaying the principal at maturity, and for preference shares it means the company buying them back, which differ from mutual fund redemption.
example: Say an investor redeems 2,000 units at an NAV of ₹50, worth ₹1,00,000. With a 1% exit load for selling within a year, ₹1,000 is deducted and ₹99,000 is paid out, before any tax.
formula: Redemption proceeds = Units redeemed × NAV × (1 − Exit load)

short: A systematic investment plan (a fixed monthly investment) whose amount rises automatically each year by a set sum or percentage.
kid: Every birthday you grow a little taller, and you also start putting one extra coin in your piggy bank each week. Small extra steps add up to a much fuller piggy bank.
detail: A step-up SIP, also called a top-up SIP, is a systematic investment plan in which the instalment rises at set intervals, usually once a year, either by a fixed amount (say ₹1,000) or a percentage (say 10%). The idea is to let investing keep pace with income: a flat SIP started early in a career becomes a smaller and smaller share of salary over time, while a step-up keeps the savings rate steady or rising. Because larger instalments are added every year, a step-up SIP builds a much bigger corpus than a flat SIP of the same starting size, though much of the difference comes from the extra money put in, not just compounding. Most Indian fund houses offer it. Common confusion: a step-up does not raise the return on money already invested; it simply adds more money each year, so it must fit your future budget.
example: Say a ₹10,000 monthly SIP steps up 10% a year: it becomes ₹11,000 in year 2 and ₹12,100 in year 3. Over three years the investor puts in 12 × (₹10,000 + ₹11,000 + ₹12,100) = ₹3,97,200, compared with ₹3,60,000 in a flat SIP.
formula: Instalment in year n = Starting instalment × (1 + Step-up rate)^(n − 1)

short: The number of systematic investment plans (fixed monthly investments) closed in a month compared with the number of new ones started.
kid: Count how many children leave the swimming class this month and how many new ones join. If more leave than join, the class is getting smaller.
detail: The SIP stoppage ratio compares the number of systematic investment plans that ended in a period, whether stopped by investors or completed at maturity, with the number of new SIPs registered in the same period. It is worked out from AMFI's monthly industry data and widely watched as a sign of retail investor confidence. A ratio well below 100% means new SIPs outnumber closures and the SIP book is growing; above 100% means more SIPs closed than started. The ratio tends to rise after market falls, when some investors lose patience. Common confusions: first, it counts SIP accounts, not money, so many small SIPs closing can push the ratio up while the total monthly SIP amount still grows. Second, matured SIPs are counted too, and data clean-ups by registrars, such as removing old inactive mandates, can cause one-off spikes that do not reflect fresh investor panic.
example: Say 60 lakh new SIPs are registered in a month while 45 lakh are stopped or mature. The SIP stoppage ratio is 45 lakh / 60 lakh = 75%, and the number of live SIPs grows by 15 lakh.
formula: SIP stoppage ratio = SIPs discontinued or matured in the period / New SIPs registered in the period × 100

short: The share of holdings two funds have in common, showing whether owning both really spreads your money across different companies.
kid: If you and your friend both bring the same sandwiches to a picnic, there is lots of food but not much variety. Bringing different food makes the picnic more fun.
detail: Portfolio overlap measures how similar two funds' holdings are. The standard method takes each stock held by both funds and adds up the smaller of its two weights; the total is the share of each portfolio that is effectively the same. Investors often hold several funds believing they are diversified, but in India many large-cap, flexi-cap, ELSS and index funds own the same leading banks, IT and energy companies, so overlap of 50% or more between two funds is common. High overlap means paying separate fees for largely the same exposure and concentrating risk in a few names. Overlap tools on fund platforms and research sites make it easy to check. Common confusion: two funds with different names, categories or fund houses can still overlap heavily, while two funds in the same category can overlap little if their managers have different styles.
example: Say Fund A holds stock X at 10% and stock Y at 8%, while Fund B holds X at 6% and Y at 12%, and they share no other stocks. Their overlap is 6% + 8% = 14%, the smaller weight of each common stock added together.
formula: Portfolio overlap = Sum over common holdings of the lower of (Weight in Fund A, Weight in Fund B)

short: The highest value a fund has reached, which it must beat again before the manager can earn another performance fee.
kid: If you once built a tower ten blocks tall, you only get a new sticker when you build one taller than ten blocks, not for building back up to ten.
detail: A high-water mark is the peak net asset value per unit, or the peak value of an investor's account, on which a performance fee has already been paid. Under a high-water mark clause, the manager earns a new performance fee only on gains above that peak. If the fund falls, it must first recover all losses before fees start again, so investors do not pay twice for the same gains. It is standard in hedge funds and used by Indian portfolio management services and Category III alternative investment funds; under SEBI rules as of 2025, PMS performance fees must be charged on a high-water mark basis. It often works alongside a hurdle rate, a minimum return the fund must earn first. Common confusion: in many structures the high-water mark is tracked per investor, so two investors who joined at different times can pay different fees in the same year.
example: Say a fund's NAV rose to $120 and the manager took a performance fee, then it fell to $100. If it recovers to $115 no fee is due, but if it reaches $130 a 20% fee applies only to the $10 above $120, or $2 per unit.
formula: Performance fee base = max(0, Current NAV − High-water mark)

short: A fee a fund manager earns as a share of the profits made for investors, often only above a minimum return.
kid: If you help a friend sell lemonade and they make extra coins, they give you a few of those extra coins as a thank-you for doing a good job.
detail: A performance fee is a payment to an investment manager based on the profits it earns, on top of the regular management fee charged on assets. The classic hedge fund model is '2 and 20': 2% of assets plus 20% of profits. Many performance fees apply only above a hurdle rate, a minimum return such as 8% or a benchmark, and only on new gains above the high-water mark, so managers are not paid twice for recovering losses. In private equity the equivalent is carried interest. In India, performance fees are common in portfolio management services and alternative investment funds, while regular mutual funds charge only an expense ratio. The fee is meant to align the manager with investors, but it can encourage extra risk-taking, since the manager shares in gains but not in losses. Common confusion: a performance fee is calculated on profit, not on the total amount invested.
example: Say a $10 million fund gains $1.5 million in a year, with an 8% hurdle ($800,000) and a 20% performance fee on returns above it. The fee is 20% × ($1,500,000 − $800,000) = $140,000.
formula: Performance fee = Fee rate × (Profit − Hurdle return), charged only on gains above the high-water mark

short: A hedge fund that splits its money among many independent trading teams running different strategies, under strict central risk limits.
kid: Imagine a big lemonade company with fifty little stands, each run by a different team. If one stand keeps losing, it is closed, and the money goes to the stands doing well.
detail: A multi-strategy hedge fund runs many strategies under one roof, such as equity long-short, fixed-income relative value, macro, commodities and quantitative trading. The largest firms, often called multi-manager platforms or 'pod shops', such as Citadel and Millennium Management, hand capital to dozens or hundreds of small teams (pods), each led by a portfolio manager. Pods are kept small and loosely related, often run with substantial leverage, and face tight drawdown limits: a pod that loses a set amount may have its capital cut or be shut down. A central risk team hedges out unwanted market exposure, aiming for steady returns with little sensitivity to stock or bond markets. Many charge pass-through fees, passing the firm's costs, including staff pay, on to investors in addition to performance fees. Common confusion: spreading money across pods reduces risk, but heavy leverage and crowded trades across rival platforms can still cause sharp losses.
example: Say a platform allocates $10 billion across 50 pods of $200 million each. If a pod's stop-loss is a 5% drawdown, it gets cut back once it loses $10 million (5% of $200 million), however strong the manager's past record.

short: India's first corporate bond ETF, launched by the government in 2019, holding top-rated bonds of state-owned companies that mature on fixed dates.
kid: Imagine lending your pocket money to some big, trusted helpers picked by the government. They promise to give it back, with a little extra, on a fixed day.
detail: Bharat Bond ETF is a series of target maturity exchange-traded funds launched by the government through DIPAM in December 2019 and managed by Edelweiss Mutual Fund. Each series tracks a Nifty Bharat Bond Index of AAA-rated bonds issued by central public sector enterprises, public sector undertakings and other government-owned entities, all maturing around the same date, for example April 2030 or April 2033. The units trade on stock exchanges, and matching fund-of-funds versions let investors without a demat account join through SIPs or lump sums. Held to maturity, an investor earns roughly the portfolio yield at purchase minus very low expenses. The April 2023 and April 2025 series have matured and repaid investors. The product helped create India's target maturity fund category and gave PSUs a new way to borrow. Common confusion: the bonds are issued by PSUs, not by the government itself, so they are not sovereign bonds.
example: Say an investor puts ₹1,00,000 into a five-year target maturity bond ETF of the Bharat Bond type when its portfolio yields 7% a year. Held to maturity at roughly that rate, before costs and tax, it grows to about ₹1,40,255 (₹1,00,000 × 1.07^5).
